φυσικός, καθ' ὃ εἴρηται ὅταν γὰρ ἔθνη τὰ μὴ νόμον ἔχοντα φύ ει τὰ τοῦ νόμου ποιῇ
καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς. λέγεται νόμος καὶ ἡ Μωσέως ἱστορία, ὡς ὅταν ἐν τῇ πρὸς Γαλάτας
φάσκῃ λέγετέ μοι οἱ τὸν νόμον ἀναγινώ κοντε τὸν νόμον οὐκ ἀκούετε, γέγραπται
γάρ, Ἀβραὰμ δύο υἱοὺ ἔ χεν καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς. καλεῖ δὲ καὶ τὰ προφητικὰ νόμον, ὡς ἐν τῷ
νόμῳ γέγραπται, ἐν ἑτερογλώ οι καὶ ἐν χείλε ιν ἑτέροι λαλή ω τῷ λαῷ τούτῳ ἐν
Ἠσαίᾳ. μήποτε δὲ καὶ τὴν Χριστοῦ περὶ τῶν πρακτέων διδασκαλίαν νόμον καλεῖ, ὡς
ὅταν φάσκῃ ἑαυτὸν μὴ ἄνομον εἶναι θεοῦ ἀλλ' ἔννομον Χρι τοῦ. ὅταν οὖν φάσκῃ
οἵτινε ἐν νόμῳ δικαιοῦ θε τῆ χάριτο ἐξεπέ ατε, ἀνατρέπει ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ τοῦ Μωσέως
γράμματος. περιτομὴν οὖν, ἣν αὐτός φησι νῦν, ἑτέραν λέγει παρὰ τὴν κατατομήν·
καὶ νόμον, τὸν πνευματικόν. δύναται δὲ νῦν νόμος νοεῖσθαι καὶ ὁ κατὰ τὰς φυσικὰς
ἐννοίας· κατὰ γὰρ τὴν τῆς ψυχῆς βελτίωσιν ὁ πνευματικῶς περιτεμνόμενος
ὠφελεῖται κατὰ τὴν τῶν φαύλων περιαίρεσιν, διὰ δὲ τοῦ πράττειν τὸν νόμον τὰ
πρακτέα ἐργαζόμενος. δύναται δέ τις καὶ κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν ἐκτὸς ἀναγωγῆς
ἐξηγήσασθαι τὸ ῥητόν, καί φησιν ὅτι πρὸς τοὺς ἀπὸ Ἰουδαίων διαλεγόμενος τοῦτό
φησιν· ἐγένετο γὰρ τοῖ Ἰουδαίοι ὡ Ἰουδαῖο ἵνα Ἰουδαίου κερδή ῃ, περιτεμὼν τὸν
Τιμόθεον καὶ κειράμενο καὶ καθαιρόμενος κατὰ νόμον, ὥστε καὶ πρὸς αὐτοὺς λέγειν
περιτομὴ μὲν γὰρ ὠφελεῖ ἐὰν νόμον πράσσῃς, πρὸς δὲ τοὺς ἐξ ἐθνῶν διαλεγόμενος
ταύτην κωλύει, μὴ ἐναντιούμενος ἑαυτῷ· ἐπειδὴ δὲ εἴρηται ἐν τῷ περὶ ταύτης λόγῳ
τῷ Ἀβραὰμ τοὺς ἐξ ἐθνῶν περιτέμνεσθαι, εἰ μὴ τοὺς ἀπὸ πέρματο αὐτοῦ, καὶ τοὺς
οἰκογενεῖ καὶ ἀργυρωνήτου · ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ἐν τῷ Λευιτικῷ περὶ τῶν υἱῶν Ἰσραὴλ
εἴρηται μόνον· οὐκ ἀνάγκη δὲ καὶ τοὺς προσηλύτους τούτοις προσυπακούεσθαι, ἐπεὶ
οὐδὲ τὰ περὶ τῶν Λευιτῶν ἰδικῶς νενομοθετημένα, ἢ τὰ περὶ τῶν ἱερέων, ἢ τὰ περὶ
τῆς γερουσίας προσυπακούειν αὐτοῖς δίδωσι καὶ ἑτέρους. ὅταν γὰρ καὶ τοὺς
προσηλύτους βούλεταί τι διαπράττεσθαι, ἰδικῶς καὶ αὐτῶν μέμνηται, ὡς ὅταν περὶ
θυσίας φησίν. ἀμέλει καὶ συνεστηκότος τοῦ καλουμένου ἁγιάσματος προσέφερον καὶ
προσήλυτοι· ὡς καὶ περὶ τῶν δέκα λεπρῶν τῶν καθαρθέντων ὁ κύριος ἔφη
πορευθέντε δείξατε ἑαυτοὺ τοῖ ἱερεῦ ιν· ἀφ' ὧν αμαρείτη εἷς ἦν. ᾧ μαρτυρῶν ὁ
σωτήρ φησιν οὐχὶ οἱ δέκα ἐκαθαρί θη αν; οἱ δὲ ἐννέα ποῦ; οὐχ εὑρέθη αν
ὑπο τρέψαντε δόξαν δοῦναι τῷ θεῷ εἰ μὴ ὁ ἀλλογενὴ οὗτο . εἰ δέ τις τὰ ἀπὸ τῆς
Ἐξόδου ἀνθυποίσει περὶ τῶν ἐσθίειν τὸ πάσχα βουλομένων προσηλύτων, ὡς δεῖ
αὐτοὺς περιτέμνεσθαι, φήσομεν ὡς ἐν ἑνὶ τόπῳ θύε θαι τὸ πά χα προσέταξεν ὁ θεός,
τούτου δὲ μὴ ἱσταμένου νῦν περιττὴ ἡ περιτομὴ τοῖς ἐξ ἐθνῶν. 11 iii 1–3 τί οὖν τὸ
περισσὸν τοῦ Ἰουδαίου, ἢ τίς ἡ ὠφέλεια τῆς περιτομῆς; πολὺ κατὰ πάντα τρόπον·
πρῶτον μὲν γὰρ ὅτι ἐπιστεύθησαν τὰ λόγια τοῦ θεοῦ. τί γὰρ εἰ ἠπίστησάν τινες; μὴ ἡ
ἀπιστία αὐτῶν τὴν πίστιν τοῦ θεοῦ καταργήσει; μὴ γένοιτο. τὸ πιστευθῆναι τὰ λόγια
τοῦ θεοῦ οὐκ ἐν τῷ βιβλία καὶ γράμματα πι στευθῆναι χαρακτηρίζεται, ἀλλ' ἐν τῷ
τὸν ἐν αὐτοῖς νοῦν καὶ τὰ ἐναποκείμενα μυστήρια γινώσκεσθαι. κατὰ γὰρ τὸν ὑγιῆ
λόγον ὁ οφὸ νοή ει τὰ ἀπὸ τοῦ ἰδίου τόματο · ἐπὶ δὲ χείλε ι φορέ ει ἐπιγνωμο ύνην.
τοιοῦτος ἦν Μωυσῆς καὶ οἱ προφῆται, Ἰουδαῖοι ὄντες καὶ πιστευθέντες τὰ λόγια τοῦ
θεοῦ, καὶ εἴ τις παρ' αὐτοῖς τούτοις παραπλήσιος. καὶ οἱ ἀπόστολοι δὲ τοῦ κυρίου
ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ εἶχον τὸ περισσὸν τοῦ Ἰουδαίου καὶ τὴν τῆς περιτομῆς
ὠφέλειαν παρὰ τοὺς ὑπ' αὐτῶν μαθόντας τὸν χριστιανισμόν. ἔστι δὲ καὶ τοῖς ἐξ
ἐθνῶν πολὺ τὸ περισσὸν παρὰ τοὺς ἐκ περιτομῆς· ἀπ' ἐκείνων γὰρ ἤρθη ἡ βα ιλεία
τοῦ θεοῦ ἵνα δοθῇ ἔθνει ποιοῦντι τοὺ καρποὺ αὐτῆ . εἰ δὲ πρῶτοι ἐκεῖνοι
ἐπιστεύθησαν τὰ λόγια τοῦ θεοῦ, εἰσὶν οἱ καὶ δεύτερον πιστευ θέντες· τὸ γὰρ πρῶτον
pass_a_gloss: Nature is spoken of when the Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature the things of the law; the law is also called the history of Moses, as when in Galatians he says to those who seek the law, do you not hear the law? For it is written, Abraham had two sons; and so on. He also calls the prophetic writings law, as it is written in the law, in other tongues and other lips they shall speak to this people, in Isaiah. Perhaps he also calls Christ's teaching about practical things law, as when he says he is not without God's law but under Christ's law. Therefore when he says those who are justified by the law are deprived of grace, he overturns us from the letter of Moses. Circumcision, which he now says, he speaks of another kind apart from the mutilation; and the law, the spiritual law. Now the law can be understood according to the natural conceptions; for according to the soul's improvement, the one who is spiritually circumcised is benefited according to the removal of the wicked, and by practicing the law, he works out the practical things. One can also interpret the spoken word externally by exposition, and he says that when speaking to those from Judea, he says this: For it happened to the Jews as a Jew that he might gain a Jew, having circumcised Timothy and shaved and purified himself according to the law, so that he might also speak to them: circumcision indeed profits if one practices the law, but to those from the Gentiles he forbids this, not acting against himself; since it has been said in the discourse about this, that the Abrahamic descendants of the Gentiles are to be circumcised, if not those from his seed, and the household-born and silver-bought; likewise in Leviticus it is said only concerning the sons of Israel, but there is no necessity that these proselytes should obey these things, since neither the things concerning the Levites specifically, nor the priests, nor the senate, are commanded to obey these things; for when he wishes to act with the proselytes, he specifically remembers them, as when he speaks of sacrifices. Moreover, when the called sanctification was established, both natives and proselytes brought offerings; as also concerning the ten lepers who were cleansed, the Lord said, Go show yourselves to the priests; from which one was healed. The Savior bears witness saying, Were not the ten cleansed? But where are the nine? Was no one found to return and give glory to God except this foreigner? And if anyone raises a question from Exodus about those who wish to eat the Passover and are proselytes, as they ought to be circumcised, we will say as in one place he commanded to sacrifice the Passover, but this not standing now, the circumcision is excessive for those from the Gentiles. 11 iii 1–3 What then is the advantage of the Jew, or what is the benefit of circumcision? Much in every way: first, that they were entrusted with the oracles of God. For if some did not believe, does their unbelief nullify the faithfulness of God? May it not be! The being entrusted with the oracles of God is not characterized by believing in books and letters, but by knowing the mind that is in them and the mysteries left behind. For according to the sound reason, the one who thinks of the things from his own taste, and on the other hand, carries on the lips epistemic knowledge. Such was Moses and the prophets, Jews who were entrusted with the oracles of God, and if anyone among them was similar. And the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ also had the advantage of the Jew and the benefit of circumcision, which they passed on to those who learned Christianity from them. And there is also much advantage for those from the Gentiles over those from circumcision; for from them the kingdom of God arose, that it might be given to a nation producing its fruits. But if those first were entrusted with the oracles of God, then they are the ones who believed second; for the first entrusting leads to second believing.
pass_b_english: When the Gentiles, who lack the written law, nevertheless fulfill its requirements by innate disposition, Paul speaks of a nature that is not merely biological but moral—a law written in the conscience. He extends the term “law” beyond the Torah of Moses to include the prophetic writings, as when he cites Isaiah: ‘In strange tongues and through foreign lips they will speak to this people.’ Even Christ’s ethical teaching, he suggests, functions as a law—not the law of Sinai, but the law of grace embodied in obedience to God through Christ. Thus, when Paul declares that those who seek justification by the law are severed from grace, he is not rejecting moral effort but overturning reliance on the external letter of Moses, which cannot impart life. Circumcision, he clarifies, is not the physical mutilation some imagine, but a spiritual reality: the cutting away of corruption from the heart. One who is inwardly circumcised by the Spirit profits not from ritual observance but from the renewal of the soul, which enables the practice of righteousness. Yet Paul also acknowledges that the law can be interpreted externally, through exposition, as when he addresses those from Judea: he became as a Jew to win Jews, having circumcised Timothy and observed ritual purity, not to compromise the gospel but to remove avoidable offense. To the Gentiles, however, he refuses to impose circumcision, not because he is inconsistent, but because the Abrahamic promise includes Gentile believers not as proselytes bound by Levitical codes, but as heirs through faith. The Levites, priests, and elders were never commanded to impose such rites on converts; God’s concern was always for the heart, not the periphery. When the sacred rites of sanctification were observed, both native Israelites and resident foreigners brought offerings—just as, when the ten lepers were cleansed, only the foreigner returned to give glory to God, prompting Jesus’ lament: ‘Were not ten made clean? Where are the nine?’ Even regarding the Passover, if a Gentile proselyte insists on observing it, Paul would say: though God once commanded its observance with circumcision, that requirement no longer stands, for the substance has been fulfilled in Christ; to insist on the outward rite now is to burden consciences with what was never meant to be eternal. Then comes the question: What advantage has the Jew? What profit is there in circumcision? Great in every respect. First, they were entrusted with the very oracles of God. Yet this privilege does not consist in mere possession of scrolls or mechanical recitation, but in perceiving the divine mind within them—the mysteries hidden beneath the surface. As sound reason teaches, the one who muses on divine things from personal inclination, and yet speaks of them with learned lips, is like Moses and the prophets: Jews who grasped the oracles not as texts but as truth. And if any among them resembled this, so too did the apostles of Christ, who inherited this Jewish advantage and passed it on to those who learned Christianity from them. But there is also a superior advantage for the Gentiles: from them the kingdom of God has arisen, destined to be given to a nation that bears its fruits. And if the Jews were first entrusted with the oracles, then they are also the first to have believed—for the divine deposit precedes human response, and faith follows the gift.

choices.choice: Paul uses 'law' flexibly to include moral conscience, prophetic writings, and Christ’s teaching—not only the Torah.
Gentile believers are not required to be circumcised or observe Levitical rites, as their inclusion is by faith, not ethnic proselytism.
